chapters.name: Chapter 1: Understanding change and bringing people with you

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Why people resist change
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the likely reasons people will resist your change, so you can respond to them.
This lesson builds toward: Given a change you want to lead, you will list who is affected and what each group may lose and gain, and the likely reasons they may resist, treating each concern as information to respond to.
Change means losing something familiar, even when the new way is better. People resist for understandable reasons: they do not see why it is needed, they fear they will not be good at the new way, they worry about losing time, money, status or friends, they were not asked, or past changes went badly.
Resistance is information, not an attack. The person pushing back often sees a real problem you missed. Treat their concern seriously and ask about it.
Before you announce anything, list who is affected and what each group may lose and gain. That list tells you what to explain, who to involve and what support to give.
Step by step:
- Write the change in one sentence.
- List every group it affects.
- For each group, write what they may lose and what they may gain.
- Mark the concerns you need to answer.
Words to know:
- Resistance: pushing back against a change, openly or quietly.
- Stakeholder: anyone affected by a change or who can affect whether it works.
Try it now: Choose a real change you want to lead. Write it in one sentence. Then list three groups it affects and, for each, one thing they may lose and one thing they may gain.
You can now predict why people may resist a change and map what each group may lose and gain.

check.q: Which is an understandable reason people resist a change?
options: They want the team to fail
check.why: Not being asked is one of the common, understandable reasons for resistance.

check.q: Before announcing a change, what would you do first?
options: Send an email to everyone at once
Ask AI to write the announcement
List who is affected and what each group may lose and gain
check.why: That list tells you what to explain, who to involve and what support to give.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making the case for change
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain in a few sentences why a change is needed, in words the people affected care about.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real change, you will write a case for change that says the problem, what will be better and what happens if you do nothing, in two or three sentences using a real fact or story.
People need to understand why before they accept what. A strong case answers three questions: What is the problem today? What will be better after the change? What happens if we do nothing?
Use facts and a real story. "Our paper sign-up sheets lost 30 volunteer names last month, and two families missed their food delivery" moves people more than "we need to modernize". Speak to what each group cares about: time, fairness, safety, customers, the people you serve.
Be honest about what is hard. If the new way takes extra work at first, say so and say how you will help. People trust a leader who admits the costs. An AI assistant can help you tighten your wording, but the facts and story should be your own.
Step by step:
- Describe the problem today, with a fact.
- Describe what will be better.
- Say what happens if nothing changes.
- Add one real story.
- Be honest about what will be hard and how you will help.
Words to know:
- Case for change: a short explanation of why a change is needed and what it will make better.
Try it now: Write your case for change in four sentences: the problem today with one fact, what will be better, what happens if nothing changes, and one honest line about what will be hard. Read it aloud. Would the people affected care?
You can now write a short, honest case for change that answers why, not just what.

check.q: Which case for change is strongest?
options: "Last month our paper forms lost 12 orders and three customers left."
check.why: A real fact and story move people more than a slogan.

check.q: The new way will take extra time at first. What would you say?
options: Say so honestly and say how you will help
check.why: People trust a leader who admits the costs.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Involving the people affected
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan how to involve the people a change affects before decisions are final.
This lesson builds toward: Given the people a change affects, you will plan how to involve them early, such as ideas, a pilot or change champions, saying what is open and what is not, and how you will report back.
People support what they help create. Involve them early, while there is still room to change the plan. Asking after everything is decided feels fake, and people can tell.
Ways to involve people: ask for their ideas in a short meeting or survey, test the change with a small group first, invite a few respected team members to help lead it, and let people choose how some parts are done.
Be clear about what is open and what is not. "We are moving to the new system by March; you can help decide how we train and in what order teams switch." Then show what you did with their input, even when you could not use it.
Step by step:
- Decide what is fixed and what is open.
- Ask for ideas early, in a meeting or short survey.
- Test with a small pilot group.
- Invite respected team members to help lead.
- Report back on what you did with the input.
Words to know:
- Pilot: a small test of a change with a few people before everyone switches.
- Change champion: a respected team member who helps lead and explain the change.
Try it now: For your change, write what is fixed and what is open. Then name two ways you will involve people and two people you could ask to be change champions.
You can now involve the people a change affects in an honest way and close the loop on their input.

check.q: Why does asking for input after everything is decided backfire?
options: It feels fake, and people can tell
check.why: Involve people while there is still room to change the plan.

check.q: You collected ideas but could not use some of them. What would you do?
options: Report back on what you did with the input and why
check.why: Showing what you did with input keeps trust, even when you could not use it.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Planning, communicating and making it stick

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a simple change plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page change plan that answers what, why, who, when, and how you will know.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real change, you will write a one-page change plan answering what, why, who, when and how you will know, with an owner for each step and two or three measures with check dates.
A change plan does not need to be long. One page that answers five questions is enough for most changes: What is changing? Why? Who is affected and who does what? When does each step happen? How will you know it is working?
"How you'll know" is the part people skip. Choose two or three signs you can actually check, such as "95% of orders entered in the new system by week 4" or "no missed deliveries for a month". Pick a date to look at them.
Name an owner for each step, plan training and support before the switch, and say what you will do if something goes wrong, like keeping the old way available for a short time.
Step by step:
- What: the change in one sentence.
- Why: your case in two or three sentences.
- Who: groups affected, and an owner for each step.
- When: key dates, including training before the switch.
- How you'll know: two or three measures and a date to check them.
- A backup plan if something goes wrong.
Words to know:
- Change plan: a short written plan saying what is changing, why, who, when and how success will be measured.
- Measure: something you can count or check to see whether a change is working.
- Owner: the one person responsible for making a step happen.
Try it now: Write the first draft of your one-page plan with all five parts. For "how you'll know", write two measures and the date you will check them.
You can now write a short change plan with clear owners, dates and measures of success.

check.q: Which part of a change plan do people most often skip?
options: How you will know it is working
check.why: Choose two or three signs you can check and a date to look at them.

check.q: You are worried the new system might fail in week one. What would you add to the plan?
options: What you will do if it goes wrong, such as keeping the old way for a short time
A second launch date in a year
check.why: A good plan says what you will do if something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Communicating the change and getting quick wins
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write clear messages for different groups and plan an early, visible win.
This lesson builds toward: When announcing a change, you will write messages for three different groups and plan one quick win, each message saying what changes, why, when, the help they get and who to ask.
Say it more than once, in more than one way. People are busy and hear a message several times before it sinks in. Use a meeting, a short written note, and one-on-one talks. Tell people affected the most first, and in person if you can, before they hear it from someone else.
Shape the message for each group: what is changing for them, why, when, what help they will get, and who to ask. Leave room for questions, and if you do not know an answer, say so and say when you will find out.
Plan a quick win: an early, visible success in the first weeks, like a shorter line or a faster report. Share it and thank the people who made it happen. Quick wins show the change is working and win over people who were unsure.
Step by step:
- Tell the most affected people first, in person if possible.
- For each group: what changes for them, why, when, help, who to ask.
- Repeat through meetings, notes and one-on-ones.
- Answer questions honestly; say when you will find out.
- Plan and celebrate one quick win in the first month.
Words to know:
- Quick win: an early, visible success that shows a change is working.
- Audience: the group of people a message is written for.
Try it now: Write three short messages about your change for three different groups (for example front-line staff, managers and customers). Then write one quick win you could show in the first month.
You can now communicate a change clearly to different groups and plan an early win that builds support.

options: Finishing the change in one day
An early, visible success that shows the change is working
A prize for the first person to switch
check.why: Quick wins win over people who were unsure.

check.q: How would you tell the people most affected by the change?
options: Let them hear it from someone else
Put a notice on the wall
Send one email to all staff
Tell them first, in person if you can
check.why: The most affected people should hear it first, before rumors reach them.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making the change stick
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan how to keep a change going after launch so people do not slide back to the old way.
This lesson builds toward: After the change launches, you will plan two ways to keep the change going, such as checking measures on set dates and building the new way into checklists or training.
Launch day is not the finish line. Many changes fade after a few weeks as people slip back to old habits, especially when they are busy or stressed.
To make it stick: check your measures on the dates you set, keep support easy to find, remove the old way once the new one works, and build the change into everyday routines like checklists, onboarding for new hires, and job expectations.
Keep listening. Ask people what is still hard and fix it. Thank people who use the new way well, and share results. When the change is part of "how we do things here", look back on what you learned for the next change.
Step by step:
- Check your measures on the planned dates.
- Keep help easy to find.
- Retire the old way when the new one works.
- Add the change to checklists, training and job expectations.
- Ask what is still hard, and fix it.
- Share results and thank people.
Words to know:
- Sustain: to keep something going over time.
- Routine: the regular way work gets done every day or week.
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page change plan. Add three messages for three groups, one quick win in the first month, and two ways you will keep the change going after launch.
You can now keep a change going after launch by checking results, building it into routines and listening to the people doing the work.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Why it matters The reason is a slogan, such as "we need to modernize". Two or three sentences on the problem, what will be better and what happens if nothing changes. Uses a real fact or story the people affected will care about. Who is affected and how they are involved No one is involved before the decision is final. Names who is affected and how they will be involved early. Says what is open and what is not, and how input will be reported back. Plan and measures Missing what, why, who, when or how you will know. Answers all five questions, with when each step happens and how you will know it is working. Each step has an owner and each measure has a check date. Messages and quick win One message for everyone, or no quick win. Three messages for three groups and one quick win in the first month. Each message says the help people will get and who to ask. Keeping it going The plan stops at launch. Two ways to keep the change going after launch. Includes building the new way into checklists, training or job expectations. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What often happens to a change a few weeks after launch?
options: It fades as people slip back to old habits
It always sticks on its own
check.why: Launch day is not the finish line; habits pull people back.

check.q: The new way works well. What would you do with the old way?
options: Remove the old way and build the new one into checklists and training
check.why: Removing the old way and building in the new one helps the change stick.
